Saturday Night Live is a groundbreaking sketch comedy and music television show that debuted on NBC in 1975 and has become the longest-running variety series in American history. Created by Lorne Michaels, the show revolutionized comedy television by building a repertory company of performers, rotating guest hosts and musical artists, and maintaining a deliberately unpredictable, occasionally anarchic energy through live broadcast that kept viewers coming back week after week.

The show premiered on NBC on October 11, 1975, at eleven-thirty p.m. on Saturday nights, launching the careers of an extraordinary roster of comedians and actors including Dan Aykroyd, Gilda Radner, Eddie Murphy, Tina Fey, and Kristen Wiig. The format consists of a five-minute monologue from a rotating guest host, followed by three to five sketch comedy segments, interspersed with music from a different musical guest each week, all performed live to a national audience. The show created the Not Ready for Prime Time Players, a stable of cast members who became household names and launched film and television careers for many of them. The show's alumni are a who's-who of contemporary comedy and entertainment.

Early seasons featured the cold open, a topical sketch that often spoofed current events or public figures, a format now imitated by nearly every sketch-comedy show. Famous recurring sketches include The Church Lady, Wayne's World, Stefon, and countless characters and catchphrases that entered the cultural lexicon and became part of American popular culture. The live format creates genuine unpredictability, moments of flubbed lines, breaking character, or creative spontaneity, which became part of the show's appeal and mystique. The program served as a launching pad for musical artists like Simon and Garfunkel and Sinead O'Connor, plus countless others who have performed on the show. Saturday Night Live has been the stage for musical breakthroughs and cultural moments for nearly fifty years.
